statements: The chief concern is acute decompensation in a previously term newborn on day 6 of life.
The newborn had tachypnea.
The newborn had sweating.
The newborn had poor feeding/failure to thrive.
The newborn had hypotension.
The newborn had metabolic/lactic acidosis.
The newborn had hepatomegaly.
The newborn had weak femoral pulses.
The newborn had evidence of heart failure.
The key diagnostic task is to explain a transient neonatal episode of myocardial ischemia/dysfunction.
The salient positive findings strongly suggest acute myocardial injury with heart failure.
Troponin T was very high at 1001 ng/L.
CK-MB was very high at 37.4 mcg/L.
Lactate was 14.8 mmol/L.
Chest imaging showed cardiomegaly with pulmonary venous congestion.
The ECG showed inferior Q waves.
The ECG showed lateral repolarization abnormalities.
TTE showed inferior wall hypokinesis.
TTE showed septal dyskinesis.
TTE showed mildly depressed left ventricular function.
TTE showed right ventricular enlargement and dysfunction.
TTE showed new moderate mitral regurgitation.
TTE showed severe tricuspid regurgitation.
The left coronary artery was initially not well visualized.
The poor visualization of the left coronary artery appropriately raises concern for congenital coronary anomaly causing ischemia.
The timing at day 6 is notable.
Closure of fetal shunts/ductus can unmask duct-dependent lesions or alter coronary perfusion physiology.
Viral studies were negative.
The negative viral studies argue against infectious myocarditis.
Selective coronary angiography confirmed normal origin and anatomy of both coronary arteries.
Normal coronary origin and anatomy argue against anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery or other structural coronary anomaly.
Hemodynamic parameters were normal on catheterization.
The ventricular dysfunction and ECG changes resolved rapidly within hours.
Rapid resolution within hours is less typical for primary cardiomyopathy or persistent structural ischemic disease.
There is no family history of heart disease.
The initial neonatal echocardiogram was otherwise normal except for tricuspid valve dysplasia with moderate tricuspid regurgitation.
The first main differential is congenital coronary anomaly causing neonatal myocardial ischemia, especially ALCAPA or ostial abnormality.
This differential fits the ischemic ECG changes.
This differential fits the elevated biomarkers.
This differential fits the regional wall motion abnormalities.
This differential fits the mitral regurgitation.
Angiography definitively showed normal coronary origins and anatomy.
Normal coronary origins and anatomy make congenital coronary anomaly unlikely.
The second main differential is acute viral myocarditis.
Acute viral myocarditis can cause heart failure.
Acute viral myocarditis can cause elevated troponin.
Acute viral myocarditis can cause ventricular dysfunction.
Acute viral myocarditis can cause ECG abnormalities.
The regional ischemic pattern is less supportive of acute viral myocarditis.
The viral studies were negative.
Very rapid normalization of function and ECG is less supportive of acute viral myocarditis.
The third main differential is duct-dependent systemic outflow obstruction/coarctation presenting after ductal closure.
Day-6 shock can fit duct-dependent systemic outflow obstruction/coarctation.
Weak femoral pulses can fit duct-dependent systemic outflow obstruction/coarctation.
Metabolic acidosis can fit duct-dependent systemic outflow obstruction/coarctation.
Preserved oxygen saturation can fit duct-dependent systemic outflow obstruction/coarctation.
Echocardiography and catheterization did not identify left-sided obstructive anatomy.
The prominent myocardial injury pattern with transient regional ischemia is not fully explained by duct-dependent systemic outflow obstruction/coarctation.
The fourth main differential is transient neonatal myocardial ischemia/infarction secondary to perinatal coronary thrombosis/embolism or vasospasm.
This diagnosis best fits the marked but reversible myocardial injury.
This diagnosis best fits the ischemic ECG changes.
This diagnosis best fits the focal wall motion abnormalities.
This diagnosis best fits the severe transient AV valve regurgitation from papillary muscle or ventricular dysfunction.
This diagnosis best fits the normal coronary anatomy on angiography.
This diagnosis best fits the rapid recovery with supportive care.
The prolonged QTc after recovery is compatible with transient ischemic myocardial insult.
In neonatal case literature, this presentation is often termed transient neonatal myocardial infarction or ischemia despite normal coronary anatomy.
The infant had a dramatic ischemic myocardial event with biomarker elevation and focal left ventricular dysfunction.
Structural coronary disease was excluded.
Recovery was rapid and near-complete.
The pattern is most consistent with transient neonatal myocardial infarction.
Transient neonatal myocardial infarction is an acute myocardial ischemia with normal coronary arteries.
The likely mechanism is transient coronary insufficiency or vasospasm rather than fixed congenital heart disease or myocarditis.
The final diagnosis is transient neonatal myocardial infarction.
